blocks.text: Premise. Zero Trust is learned fastest on real systems. If you already do Zero Trust work, that work is the classroom. If you don't yet, pick one system you know well and practice on it every week.

Structure. Weeks 1 to 4 are a core that everyone takes: the definition (NIST SP 800-207) and the shared maturity scale (the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model). Weeks 5 to 8 are one track, picked by who sets your Zero Trust rules:

items: DoW track. For Department of War (DoW) components and the programs that report to them.
Federal civilian track. For federal civilian agencies and the teams that build and run their systems.
Private sector track. For companies, and also state and local governments, universities and anyone else with no federal Zero Trust mandate.

blocks.text: Not sure which? The "Which track are you?" table below settles it.
Time. About 3 hours a week in the core, and 3 to 5 in your track. One hour on weekdays, or two longer blocks.
What you will be able to do by the end of Week 8.

items: Explain Zero Trust, and the roadmap that governs your organization, in one breath, to any stakeholder, without notes.
Take one capability, such as multi-factor authentication, and walk it across the frameworks that apply to you, out loud.
Tell a security idea from a Zero Trust idea on sight, and say the Zero Trust version.

blocks.text: Field notes. Keep one text file, one line per session: Learned / Source / Where it bit us. The template is in Part 6. In three months it is your field manual, in your own words.

Naming. Executive Order 14347 authorizes Department of War (DoW) as a secondary title; the statutory name is still Department of Defense. Published document titles still say "DoD," so this guide uses DoW in prose and DoD in titles and citations.
Which track are you?

blocks.text: Everyone takes the core. It is the vocabulary every track borrows.
Each card says what the document is, why it matters, what to read, what to skip, and the one sentence you should be able to say afterward.

items.title: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture (NIST, August 2020)
bullets: What it is. The foundational definition. The tenets of Zero Trust, the logical components (policy engine, policy administrator, policy enforcement point), deployment models, and the trust algorithm.

Why it matters. Everyone borrows its vocabulary: DoW, federal civilian and commercial Zero Trust documents all build on it. When someone says PDP or PEP in a meeting, this is the document most people learned the words from.

Read. Section 2 (tenets and the Zero Trust view of a network) and Section 3 (logical components, deployment variations, trust algorithm). About 19 pages. In Week 2, skim Section 4 (use cases) and Section 7 (migration).
Skip for now. Section 5 threats (skim later); the appendices.
Be able to say. Zero Trust means every access request is decided by a policy engine on identity, device posture and context, enforced at a PEP, with no trust implied by where the request comes from.
Time. 6 hours. Weeks 1 and 2.

items.title: CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0 (CISA, April 2023)
bullets: What it is. Five pillars (Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications and Workloads, Data), three cross-cutting capabilities (Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, Governance), and four stages (Traditional, Initial, Advanced, Optimal), with a stage description for every function.

Why it matters. It is the closest thing to a shared maturity scale. CISA wrote it for federal civilian agencies, and OMB M-22-09 organizes its goals by it. It is public, so private-sector teams can borrow its stages as a target.

Read. The introduction, the stage definitions, and the five pillar chapters in Week 3. The cross-cutting capabilities in Week 4. Read for vocabulary and structure; you do not need the functions memorized.
Skip for now. Nothing. It is short enough to read whole.
Be able to say. Five pillars, three cross-cutting capabilities, four stages, and which pillar and stage one of your own controls sits at, and why.
Time. 6 hours. Weeks 3 and 4.

DoW track
For DoW components, and the programs and teams that report to them.

items.title: DoD Zero Trust Strategy (DoD CIO, October 2022)
bullets: What it is. The Department's mandate: the vision, four strategic goals, the seven pillars, Target Level and Advanced Level, and the FY27 deadline for Target.
Why it matters. It sets the destination for every DoW component: seven pillars, and a Target Level due by the end of FY27. Every other DoW Zero Trust document points back to it.
Read. Executive summary and the strategy sections on goals, pillars and the Target and Advanced split. About 20 pages.
Skip for now. Governance and organizational sections, including the material on the DoD ZT Portfolio Management Office.
Be able to say. DoW requires Target Level Zero Trust across every component by the end of FY27, and Target is 91 of the 152 activities.
Time. 2 hours. Week 5.

items.title: DoD Zero Trust Capabilities and Activities (DoD CIO ZT PfMO, as of 18 March 2025)
bullets: What it is. The yardstick. Seven pillars, 45 capabilities, 152 activities, each with outcomes, a level (Target or Advanced), and an end state.

Get the right file. The current activity list is the hyphenated ZT-CapabilitiesActivities.pdf. An older file at the similar, unhyphenated address served an earlier edition (6 January 2023); that link is now dead. Check the cover date before you trust a copy.
Why it matters. It is the full catalog behind the Strategy: 45 capabilities and 152 activities, each with published outcomes. Learn its numbering, because every other DoW document uses it.
Read. One or two pillars a week, in this order: User, Device; Network; Application and Workload, Data; Automation and Orchestration, Visibility and Analytics.
Skip for now. Nothing. But do not try to memorize outcomes. Memorize the capability names and the Target count per pillar; the outcomes are what your notes are for.
Be able to say. The capabilities in each pillar from memory, and the Target count per pillar (table in Part 5).
Time. 6 hours across Weeks 5 to 8.

items.title: NSA Zero Trust Implementation Guidelines: Primer, Discovery Phase, Phase One, Phase Two (NSA Cybersecurity Technical Reports, January 2026)
bullets: What it is. NSA's sequencing of the DoW Target activities into phases with dependencies: Discovery (14 activities), Phase One (36), Phase Two (41). Phases Three and Four will cover the Advanced activities; NSA says they "may be developed at a later date." Status checked 30 September 2026.
Why it matters. It is NSA's practical companion to the activity list, grouped into phases you can read in order.
Read. Primer, Discovery Phase and Phase One in full. Phase Two: the activity roster and the dependency notes.

Be able to say. Discovery is the inventories and analyses (users, devices, applications, data, flows, policies); Phase One is the foundational controls on top of them; Phase Two builds out and integrates. Fourteen, thirty-six, forty-one.
Time. 4 hours. Week 6.

items.title: DoD Zero Trust Reference Architecture v2.0 (DISA and NSA for DoD CIO, July 2022)
bullets: What it is. The architecture behind the strategy: principles, pillar target states, capability taxonomy, and the operational and system views. Long and dense.
Why it matters. It is where "what good looks like" is written for each capability. When a system owner asks what Target actually means for their system, the answer is here.

Read. Section 1 (purpose and strategic goals), the principles, and the User, Device and Network pillar descriptions in Section 2. Glance at the capability taxonomy so you recognize it as the parent of the 45.
Skip for now. The operational and system views beyond a glance; the appendices.

Be able to say. One sentence per pillar describing the target state. For example: Network at Target means data flows are mapped, the enterprise is macro-segmented, and critical workloads are micro-segmented on identity, with policy applied programmatically.
Time. 4 hours. Week 7.

Federal civilian track
For federal civilian agencies, and the teams that build and run their systems.

items.title: Executive Order 14028, Improving the Nation's Cybersecurity (White House, May 2021), Section 3
bullets: What it is. The root mandate. Section 3 says the federal government must advance toward Zero Trust Architecture, and gave each agency head 60 days to develop a plan to implement it.

Why it matters. Every federal civilian Zero Trust requirement traces back to it. Later executive orders changed other parts of the cybersecurity agenda; Section 3's Zero Trust direction still stands, as checked 30 September 2026.
Read. Section 3, Modernizing Federal Government Cybersecurity. About 3 pages.
Be able to say. EO 14028 directed the move to Zero Trust; M-22-09 set the targets.
Time. 1 hour. Week 5.

items.title: OMB Memorandum M-22-09, Moving the U.S. Government Toward Zero Trust Cybersecurity Principles (OMB, January 2022)
bullets: What it is. The federal Zero Trust strategy. It sets specific goals for every executive department and agency, due by the end of fiscal year 2024, organized by the five pillars of the CISA maturity model.

Why it matters. It is the most concrete statement of what federal civilian Zero Trust means: enterprise identities with phishing-resistant MFA, a complete device inventory with detection and response, encrypted DNS and HTTP traffic with a plan to break down perimeters, applications treated as internet-connected and tested, and data protection built on categorization.
Read. All of it. Read the five pillar goals twice.
Watch. Its deadline, the end of FY2024, has passed. No rescission was found as of 30 September 2026. Check OMB's memoranda page and the current FISMA guidance for what agencies report now.
Be able to say. The M-22-09 goal for each of the five pillars, in one sentence each.
Time. 3 hours. Week 5.

items.title: OMB Memorandum M-26-14, Ensuring Effective and Efficient Agency Logging and Network Visibility to Defend Against Evolving Cyber Threats (OMB, May 2026)
bullets: What it is. The current federal logging memo. It rescinded the earlier logging memo, M-21-31, and aligns its logging requirements with the CISA maturity model.
Why it matters. Visibility is a cross-cutting capability in the CISA model, and logging is where it becomes a requirement.
Read. The requirements sections, and how they map to the maturity model.
Be able to say. Which memo sets federal logging requirements today, and how it connects to the maturity model.
Time. 2 hours. Week 6.

items.title: CISA, Microsegmentation in Zero Trust, Part One: Introduction and Planning (CISA, July 2025)
bullets: What it is. CISA's guide to moving from perimeter security to microsegmentation, part of its "Journey to Zero Trust" series. It lays out a four-phase approach and the planning considerations that go with it. A technical implementation part is planned.
Why it matters. Networks is the pillar where M-22-09 asked agencies to start breaking down perimeters. This is the how.
Read. All of it.
Be able to say. Why microsegmentation limits lateral movement, and the first thing you would plan before segmenting anything.
Time. 3 hours. Week 7.

items.title: Federal Zero Trust Data Security Guide (Federal CISO Council and CDO Council, October 2024, revised May 2025)
bullets: What it is. Practical guidance on defining, securing and managing data through its lifecycle, focused on the Data pillar of the CISA maturity model. The May 2025 revision added a chapter.
Why it matters. Data is often the pillar programs reach last, and it depends on the categorization M-22-09 asked for.
Read. The chapters on defining and securing data.
Be able to say. Why data categorization comes before data protection tools.
Time. 3 hours. Week 8.

Private sector track
For companies, and for state and local governments, universities and anyone else with no federal Zero Trust mandate.

Start here. No federal Zero Trust mandate binds you, unless a contract or regulator names a framework. In that case, start from the framework they named. Otherwise the pattern is: use the Cybersecurity Framework to say what good looks like, SP 800-207 to define Zero Trust, the CISA maturity model to set a target, and SP 1800-35 to see how others built it.

items.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 (NIST, February 2024)
bullets: What it is. A taxonomy of cybersecurity outcomes for any organization, of any size or sector. Six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

Why it matters. It is the language boards and auditors already use. Zero Trust work lands mostly in Protect (identity management, authentication and access control) and Detect, and it is steered by Govern.
Read. The overview of the six functions, and the Govern and Protect sections of the core.
Be able to say. The six functions, and which of them a Zero Trust program mostly serves.
Time. 3 hours. Week 5.

items.title: NIST SP 1800-35, Implementing a Zero Trust Architecture (NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence, June 2025)
bullets: What it is. NIST's practice guide: 19 example Zero Trust implementations built with 24 collaborators, with lessons learned and mappings to common security standards.
Why it matters. It turns the SP 800-207 model into working builds. It is the closest thing to seeing how other organizations actually did it.
Read. The high-level document, then the example build closest to your own environment.
Skip for now. The builds unlike your environment.
Be able to say. How one example build places the PDP and the PEPs, and what it would take to do the same in your environment.
Time. 4 hours. Week 6.

items.title: CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0, as your target (CISA, April 2023)
bullets: What it is. You read it in the core. On this track you use it as a target: pick a stage per pillar and write it down.
Why it matters. Without a mandate, you need a target you chose on purpose. Borrowing a public one makes it easy to explain.
Read. Re-read the stage tables for the pillars that matter most to your organization.
Be able to say. Your target stage per pillar, and why you chose it.
Time. 2 hours. Week 7.

items.title: CISA, Microsegmentation in Zero Trust, Part One: Introduction and Planning (CISA, July 2025)
bullets: What it is. CISA's guide to moving from perimeter security to microsegmentation. It names federal civilian agencies but says any organization can apply it.
Why it matters. Segmentation is often where private-sector programs spend their first real Zero Trust money.
Read. All of it.
Be able to say. Why microsegmentation limits lateral movement, and the first thing you would plan before segmenting anything.
Time. 3 hours. Week 7 or 8.

chapters.title: Part 3. The eight weeks at a glance

cells: NIST 800-207, skim Sections 4 and 7; pick your track
CISA ZTMM: stages and five pillars

blocks.text: If a week slips, do not double up. Push the plan a week and keep the order; the order is the point.
Fluency 1. Zero Trust in one breath
Say it until it comes out at conversational speed. Then say it to someone. Everyone learns the core version; add your track's version.

Core. Zero Trust means no user, device or network location is trusted by default. Every request for a resource is decided by policy, on identity, device posture and context, and enforced and logged at the point of access. NIST SP 800-207 defines it; the CISA maturity model measures it in five pillars, three cross-cutting capabilities and four stages.

DoW. DoW's Zero Trust roadmap has seven pillars: User, Device, Application and Workload, Data, Network and Environment, Automation and Orchestration, and Visibility and Analytics. Under them sit 45 capabilities and 152 activities. Ninety-one are Target Level, due across the Department by the end of FY27; sixty-one are Advanced and come after. Each activity has published outcomes, and meeting every one is the Target bar.

Federal civilian. Executive Order 14028 moved the federal government toward Zero Trust in 2021. OMB M-22-09 set goals for every agency across the five CISA pillars: enterprise identities with phishing-resistant MFA, a full device inventory, encrypted traffic and smaller perimeters, applications treated as internet-connected, and data protection built on categorization. CISA's maturity model measures progress, and newer memos, like the 2026 logging memo, build on it.

Private sector. No federal Zero Trust mandate binds us, so we chose our own target. We use the Cybersecurity Framework to describe what good looks like, NIST SP 800-207 to define Zero Trust, the CISA maturity model to set a target stage per pillar, and NIST's example builds in SP 1800-35 to see how others got there.
Drill. Time yourself. Under 45 seconds, with no filler words, and you are there. If a number wobbles, it is in Part 5.
Fluency 2. The capability walk
Take one capability and cross every framework that applies to you. A worked example: multi-factor authentication. Everyone does the core rows; then add your track's row.

cells: Authentication is part of every access decision: the policy engine weighs identity and context, and the PEP enforces the result per session.

Identity pillar, Authentication function. In broad strokes: Traditional is passwords or MFA on some systems; Advanced is phishing-resistant MFA broadly; Optimal is continuous validation with risk analysis.

Capability 1.3 MFA, User pillar. Target activity 1.3.1 Organizational MFA/IdP: an enterprise identity provider with MFA for critical applications and services, using DoD PKI and approved alternatives by resource risk level. NSA ZIG: Phase One. NSA advises completing Discovery activity 1.1.1 (inventory users) first, because you cannot enforce MFA against identities you have not enumerated.
M-22-09's Identity goal: agency staff use enterprise-managed identities, protected by phishing-resistant MFA.
CSF 2.0, Protect function: identity management, authentication and access control. SP 1800-35's example builds show how an enterprise identity provider feeds the access decision.
Legacy applications that manage their own accounts. They sit outside the enterprise identity provider, so MFA never reaches them. An honest identity inventory should expose every one.

blocks.text: Practice on: device compliance before access; data flow mapping; data loss prevention; the policy decision point; log collection and correlation. Do one per week from Week 3. Write each walk in your field notes; the writing is the drill.
Fluency 3. Security idea or Zero Trust idea?

The test. A Zero Trust idea is about a per-request access decision, made on identity, device posture and context, enforced and logged, or about the inventory, tag or policy that feeds one. A security idea is about whether a control exists or a practice is followed. Both matter. Only the first is Zero Trust.

cells: Device compliance, including endpoint detection and protection status, is checked before each access decision, and non-compliant access is denied by default.
There is a network access control solution.
Devices are authenticated and posture-checked at connection, with non-compliant devices quarantined, across every part of the environment.
Data objects are tagged to one standard, so that access decisions, data loss prevention and rights management consume the tags.
All applications authenticate through the enterprise identity provider with MFA matched to resource risk, and you know which applications still hold their own accounts.
Data flows are mapped, enclaves are macro-segmented, and critical workloads are micro-segmented on identity, with policy changes applied programmatically.
Logs from all sources are parsed to a standard schema, with baseline alerting, asset correlation, and user and device baselines feeding it.
Every action the agent takes is authorized outside the model, against the scope the user delegated, and logged by the enforcement point rather than by the agent.

blocks.text: Drill. Take any security idea you hear this week and say its Zero Trust version out loud. If you can't, find its pillar in the CISA model and try again.

blocks.text: Terms

cells: Policy engine decides, policy administrator issues, policy enforcement point allows or blocks each access (NIST SP 800-207). PDP = PE + PA.
Policy information point: the sources a decision draws on (identity, device posture, threat intelligence, data tags).
Identity provider; Identity, Credential and Access Management, the enterprise program identity rides on.
MFA that a fake login page cannot capture and replay, such as FIDO2 security keys or PKI smart cards.
Attribute-based versus role-based access control. Zero Trust wants attributes driving decisions.
Just-in-time and just-enough administration: privilege granted for the task and the window, not standing.
Unified endpoint management and mobile device management: the compliance and inventory engine for devices.
Endpoint (and extended) detection and response; feeds device compliance and the SIEM.
Software defined networking: the control plane separated from the data plane, so segmentation is programmable.
Macro: between enclaves and sites. Micro: per application or workload, identity-aware.
Data, applications, assets, services: the things a PEP protects.
Data loss prevention and digital rights management: enforcement points that consume data tags.
Log correlation and alerting; automated response playbooks; user and entity behavior baselines.
Federal civilian executive branch: the agencies M-22-09 and CISA's guidance mostly address.
Controlled unclassified information: sensitive government information that contractors must protect under NIST SP 800-171.
Comply to Connect: a device is identified, posture-checked and authorized before it gets network access; a non-compliant device is quarantined.

blocks.text: Everyone

items: NIST SP 800-207A (September 2023). Zero Trust access control for cloud-native applications, once cloud environments come into scope.

Zero Trust for AI Systems (Coalition for Secure AI, September 2026). How the same ideas apply when an AI agent acts for a user: the model sits inside its own threat boundary and is never trusted to make authorization decisions, every tool call is authorized outside the model against the user's delegated scope, and the paper gives a three-step maturity path for getting there. For the red, blue and purple team view, see the Agentic SecOps playbook.

Zero Trust in the Age of AI (my companion notebook). A NotebookLM notebook built on this guide's sources, the 2025 to 2026 guidance on AI agents and recorded talks, including transcripts of five government talks from the 2026 DoW Zero Trust Virtual Learning Exchange. chapters.title: Zero Trust Quick Reference: Federal Civilian

blocks.text: Public edition v2.8.3, 18 October 2026. Public sources only. Ken Connell.
The chain
EO 14028 (May 2021), Section 3: move to Zero Trust Architecture; every agency plans it.
OMB M-22-09 (January 2022): the federal Zero Trust strategy. Specific goals for every agency, due by the end of FY2024, organized by the five CISA pillars.
CISA ZTMM 2.0 (April 2023): how progress is measured. 5 pillars + 3 cross-cutting capabilities; 4 stages: Traditional, Initial, Advanced, Optimal.
OMB M-26-14 (May 2026): federal logging and network visibility. Rescinded M-21-31; aligns logging with the ZTMM.
Zero Trust in one breath

Executive Order 14028 moved the federal government toward Zero Trust in 2021. OMB M-22-09 set goals for every agency across the five CISA pillars: enterprise identities with phishing-resistant MFA, a full device inventory, encrypted traffic and smaller perimeters, applications treated as internet-connected, and data protection built on categorization. CISA's maturity model measures progress, and newer memos build on it.
M-22-09 goals by pillar

cells: Complete device inventory; prevent, detect and respond on every device
Encrypt DNS and HTTP traffic; start breaking perimeters into isolated environments
Treat every application as internet-connected; test rigorously; welcome external vulnerability reports
A shared path to protections built on thorough data categorization
Federal ZT Data Security Guide (Oct 2024, rev. May 2025)
Visibility and Analytics (cross-cutting; not an M-22-09 pillar goal)
Logging and network visibility, now set by OMB M-26-14

blocks.text: Maturity stages (CISA ZTMM 2.0)

Traditional: manual, static, siloed. Initial: starting automation and cross-pillar integration. Advanced: automated, centralized, cross-pillar. Optimal: fully automated, dynamic, continuously optimized.
Security idea or Zero Trust idea?
A Zero Trust idea is about a per-request access decision made on identity, device posture and context, enforced and logged, or about the inventory, tag or policy that feeds one.

"MFA is required" is a security idea. "All applications authenticate through the agency identity provider with phishing-resistant MFA, and you know which still hold their own accounts" is the Zero Trust version (Identity).
Terms

cells: Federal civilian executive branch: the agencies M-22-09 and CISA's guidance mostly address.

MFA a fake login page cannot capture and replay, such as FIDO2 keys or PKI smart cards.
Identity provider; Identity, Credential and Access Management program.
Dividing a network into small, controlled zones so a breach cannot easily move laterally.
Knowing what data you hold and how sensitive it is, so protections can use it.

The pattern

blocks.text: If a contract or regulator names a framework, start from that one.
Zero Trust in one breath

No federal Zero Trust mandate binds us, so we chose our own target. We use the Cybersecurity Framework to describe what good looks like, NIST SP 800-207 to define Zero Trust, the CISA maturity model to set a target stage per pillar, and NIST's example builds in SP 1800-35 to see how others got there.
The seven tenets (NIST SP 800-207, in short)

items: Every data source and computing service is a resource.
All communication is secured, wherever it comes from.
Access is granted per session, per resource.
Access is decided by dynamic policy: identity, application or service, device, behavior and environment.
Every asset's integrity and security posture is monitored and measured.
Authentication and authorization are dynamic and enforced before access.
Collect as much as you can about assets, network and communications, and use it to improve.

blocks.text: Where Zero Trust lands in CSF 2.0

items: Govern: the strategy, the target, who owns it.
Identify: the inventories: users, devices, applications, data, flows.
Protect: identity management, authentication and access control; data security; platform security.
Detect: continuous monitoring that feeds access decisions.
Respond and Recover: containment is easier when access is already segmented and per-request.

blocks.text: Your target (CISA ZTMM 2.0)
Mark the stage you are aiming for in each pillar. Write one line of why.
Security idea or Zero Trust idea?
A Zero Trust idea is about a per-request access decision made on identity, device posture and context, enforced and logged, or about the inventory, tag or policy that feeds one.

"The network is segmented" is a security idea. "Data flows are mapped, and critical workloads are segmented on identity, with policy changes applied automatically" is the Zero Trust version (Networks).
Handling CUI for a DoW contract?
Your security requirements come from NIST SP 800-171 and the DoW CMMC program. Zero Trust can help you meet them, but it does not replace them.
Terms

cells: Policy engine decides, administrator issues, enforcement point allows or blocks each request. PDP = PE + PA.
Policy information points: identity, device posture, threat intelligence, data tags.
Identity provider: where users sign in once, and where MFA lives.
MFA a fake login page cannot capture and replay, such as FIDO2 keys.
Small, controlled network zones, so a breach cannot easily move laterally.
NIST's National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence, which built the SP 1800-35 examples.
Controlled unclassified information: sensitive government information contractors must protect.
